title: Sliding Window: Max Sum Subarray of Size K
oneLiner: Don't recompute the whole window every time -- slide it: subtract what leaves, add what enters.
keyTakeaway: Recomputing a window's sum from scratch every time you move it is O(n*k). Sliding the window instead -- subtract the element leaving on the left, add the element entering on the right -- turns that into O(n) total: the whole array is visited a constant number of times, not once per window.
explanation: Build the first window's sum normally (add up the first k elements). Then, to move the window one step to the right, don't recompute the sum -- just subtract the element that's now outside the window on the left, and add the new element that just entered on the right. Track the best sum seen across all windows as you go. This is the fixed-size version of the sliding window pattern; a variable-size version (grow the window until some condition breaks, then shrink it) is the same core idea applied to problems like "longest substring without repeating characters." Watch out for the classic off-by-one: the window [left, right] has size (right - left + 1), not (right - left).

recognitionSignals: The problem is about a CONTIGUOUS subarray or substring (not any subset -- contiguous specifically).
There's a size constraint ("subarray of size k") or a condition to maintain ("no repeated characters", "sum <= target").
The brute-force solution recomputes something for every possible window -- that recomputation is usually avoidable by sliding.
gotchas: Window size is (right - left + 1), not (right - left) -- an easy off-by-one.
For a FIXED-size window, only start updating "best so far" once the window has reached full size k, not before.
For a VARIABLE-size window (not this lesson, but the more common real-world version), remember to shrink from the left while a condition is violated, not just grow from the right.
confusableWith: Two Pointers (this track) also uses two indices into an array, but they move toward each other from opposite ends; sliding window's two indices move in the SAME direction as the window slides forward. The tell: pair from two ends (two pointers) vs. a contiguous range that grows/slides (sliding window).

complexity.note: Each element enters the window once and leaves once -- add the new element, subtract the old one -- instead of re-summing k elements every position (which would be O(n·k)).

referenceSolutions.python:
def max_sum_subarray(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]  # slide: one in, one out
        best = max(best, window)
    return best
